sec.title: Background
sec.p: For patients with untreated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), chemotherapy before surgery (“neoadjuvant therapy”) has shown benefit in reducing recurrence and prolonging survival. Targeting the vitamin D receptor (VDR) with analogs such as paricalcitol may improve chemotherapy effectiveness. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of neoadjuvant albumin-bound paclitaxel (nab-paclitaxel) plus cisplatin plus gemcitabine (NABPLAGEM) plus paricalcitol (NCT03138720).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Participants were ≥18 years, had stage I-III PDAC without prior chemotherapy or radiation, Karnofsky Performance Status ≥70, and elevated CA 19-9. Study treatment included nab-paclitaxel (125 mg/m2), cisplatin (25 mg/m2), gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2), and paricalcitol (25 mcg) on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle for up to 6 months. The primary outcome was CA 19-9 normalization. Secondary outcomes included margin-negative resection (R0), pathologic complete response (pCR), radiologic response, safety, and survival. Microbiome was analyzed as an exploratory outcome.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Thirty-two participants were enrolled with median age 69.4 years, 56.2% male, and 93.8% white. Patients had resectable (cohort A, n = 10) and borderline resectable/locally advanced (cohort B, n = 22) tumors. CA 19-9 normalization occurred in 14 patients (43.8%). Two patients (6.2%) achieved pCR, and 19 (59.4%) achieved R0. Complete or partial radiologic response occurred in 39.3% of patients. Adverse events included grade 3-4 anemia (43.8%) and thrombocytopenia (59.4%). Median (95% CI) overall survival was 43.2 (7.5–upper bound not achieved) and 18.4 (10.9-41.2) months for cohorts A and B, respectively.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Neoadjuvant NABPLAGEM plus paricalcitol demonstrated a high CA 19-9 normalization rate and was fairly well tolerated.
Keywords: neoadjuvant therapy, pancreatic cancer, CA-19-9 antigens, paricalcitol, microbiome
Received 2026 Mar 2; Accepted 2026 Jun 5; Collection date 2026 Jul.

list-item.p: The regimen NABPLAGEM (albumin-bound paclitaxel, cisplatin, gemcitabine) with the vitamin D receptor analog paricalcitol achieved a higher CA 19-9 marker normalization rate of 43.8% in resectable, borderline resectable and locally advanced pancreas cancer compared to previous studies and could be considered as a primary endpoint in future studies.

Our trial showed a median overall survival of 19.6 months and 2-year survival of 46.9%, demonstrating that neoadjuvant multi-agent therapy did not increase symptom burden and maintained an acceptable safety profile.

tr.td: Eligible patients had histologically or cytologically confirmed resectable, borderline resectable or locally advanced PDAC; were ≥18 years old; had no prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy; KPS ≥70%; and an elevated CA 19-9 (>2× ULN).
Single-center, single-arm, investigator-initiated phase II clinical trial with resectable disease in cohort A and borderline resectable/locally advanced disease in cohort B
R0 rate; pCR rate; radiologic response rate; OS; safety

list-item.p: Additional details of endpoints or study design
Exploratory endpoints: Pain and quality of life comparisons; gut microbiome analysis; perfusion imaging

Baseline patient characteristics were compared between cohorts using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (continuous or ordinal variables) or chi-square tests (categorical variables). Differences between cohorts in rates of CA 19-9 normalization, margin-negative resection (R0), pathologic complete response (pCR), and radiologic response were tested using chi-square tests. Median (95% CI) survival time was calculated for each cohort using the Kaplan–Meier method. Statistical tests were 2-tailed, with a significance level of 0.05, and no adjustments were made for multiple comparisons. Statistical analyses were conducted using Stata SE 19.5 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Safety with adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) were assessed by the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI CTCAE) version 4.0.1 For perfusion imaging, computed tomography (CT) multiphase images were acquired with the majority using a multi-slice CT scanner (GE) with standard pancreatic protocol, which included pre-injection, arterial, portal venous phases and the iodinated contrast agent Isovue 370. GE AW 3.2 USA; a 3D imaging software application, was used to conduct the volumetric analysis.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Pancreatic cancer remains a substantial public health burden in the United States. As the third leading cause of cancer fatalities, 2026 projections anticipate nearly 67,530 new cases and 52,740 deaths.3 Despite advances, relative 5-year survival rate is poor at 13%, highlighting the limited impact of existing therapies and a persistent unmet clinical need.3,4

Due to the lack of established screening protocols, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is often diagnosed at advanced metastatic stages, with only 15% and 28% at localized and regional stages.4 Consequently, few patients are eligible for surgery with curative intent. For resectable disease, standard management is surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy, although neoadjuvant therapy remains an option. For individuals with borderline resectable (BRPC) or locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC), systemic therapy or a clinical trial is preferred.5 Current standard-of-care pre-operative regimens consist of 4 to 6 months of FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel followed by chemoradiation or stereotactic body radiation.5

While neoadjuvant therapy for PDAC has remained controversial, its adoption has steadily increased. Evidence supports improved margin-negative resection (R0) rates, reduced margin-positive resection (R1) rates, and reduced recurrence in resectable disease with improved treatment of micrometastasis in unresectable disease.6 However, there remains debate on selection criteria, chemotherapy regimens, and whether it delays or prevents initially resectable disease from upfront curative surgery.7

The use of NABPLAGEM has already been studied in advanced PDAC. A Phase Ib/II trial of untreated stage IV patients showed promising progression-free survival (PFS) of 10.1 months and an overall response rate (ORR) of 71%.8,9 Another untreated advanced Phase II trial showed 40.5% ORR and quality of life improvement in the first 3 cycles.10,11 Given that NABPLAGEM showed early disease control in the metastatic population, it was postulated to be suitable in the neoadjuvant setting.

Vitamin D receptor (VDR) analogs have emerged as a potential therapeutic approach for pancreatic cancer. In a mouse model, the addition of calcipotriol decreased tumor size, decreased fibrosis, prolonged survival, and increased gemcitabine median concentration by over 500% in tumor cells.12 Paricalcitol effectively inhibited growth of 3 human pancreatic cell lines both in vitro and in vivo when administered 3 times per week at doses that avoided hypercalcemia.13 Paricalcitol exposure in combination with gemcitabine and hydroxychloroquine additionally modulated macrophage populations and T cell activation.14 Results from a study of on treatment paired biopsies with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel alone and in combination with either oral or IV paricalcitol are pending but may provide insight on VDR activation in PDAC.15 Given VDR agonist efficacy in preclinical studies, we aimed to evaluate paricalcitol’s efficacy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

The median (range) number of treatment cycles completed was 5.5 (2-8); cohort A, 3.5 (3-6); cohort B, 6 (2-8). Twenty patients underwent surgical resection (Figure 1); 19 (59.4%) achieved R0, with 90.0% in cohort A compared to 45.5% in cohort B (P = .017). Only one patient had R1 and 2 patients achieved pCR, all in cohort B. Our 90% R0 compares favorably to 85% in the resectable PDAC SWOG study.16,17

sec.p: CA 19-9 normalization has not traditionally been used as a primary endpoint in localized PDAC trials but has demonstrated a relative survival benefit in retrospective studies.18 In our trial, CA 19-9 normalized in 14 patients (Tables 1 and 2). This 43.8% rate exceeds normalization with FOLFIRINOX (22%) and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (20%) in resectable, BRPC, and LAPC.19 Our study’s median OS of 43.2 months in the resectable group (Figure 2) is comparable to previous studies of 43 months,20 whereas 18.4 months was lower in BRPC/LAPC compared to 27.9 months.21,22 Eleven patients (39.3%) showed radiologic response (Table 3).23

sec.p: Regarding safety, NABPLAGEM plus paricalcitol was fairly well tolerated. Most AEs were lower grade and managed with dose reduction or supportive care (Tables 4 and 5).1,24 Thrombocytopenia and anemia were similar to the prior metastatic trial.10,11 Most SAEs were unrelated to NABPLAGEM (SAEs Table). No SAEs were attributed to paricalcitol, supporting its safety in combination therapy although its specific contribution is difficult to discern without a chemotherapy-only control arm. Both BPI scores, and 2 of 3 MDASI scores, improved in BRPC/LAPC (no significant change in other group; minimal baseline symptoms) (Table S1). The other MDASI score (overall symptom interference) worsened in the resectable group (no significant change in other group).

sec.p: The neoadjuvant regimen did not cause gut microbiome disruption, as overall composition and diversity remained stable from baseline to end of treatment (EOT) (Tables S2 and S3).25 However, when stratified by best overall response, significant differences in microbial community structure emerged (Figure 3). A less phylogenetically diverse gut microbiome may be associated with better response, although the small complete response sample size (n = 4) limits interpretation (Tables S4 and S5).

caption.p: Gut microbiome alpha and beta diversity by clinical response. PCoA plots representing beta diversity based on (A) Jaccard, (B) Bray-Curtis, (C) Unweighted UniFrac, and (D) Weighted UniFrac dissimilarity measures. Alpha diversity comparisons are shown via (E) Shannon Diversity and (F) Faith’s Phylogenetic Diversity indices. Data are grouped by best overall response. Statistical significance for alpha diversity was determined by Kruskal–Wallis tests, and beta diversity clustering was assessed via PERMANOVA. BOR, best overall response; PCoA, principal coordinate analysis; PD, phylogenetic diversity; PERMANOVA, permutational multivariate analysis of variance.

graphic.alt-text: Graphical representation of microbiome diversity results with subfigures A through F, grouped by best overall response.

sec.p: ANCOM-BC determined the differential microbial features.26 Partial responders showed enrichment of certain Firmicutes and depletion of Dorea formicigenerans, Desulfovibrio, and Akkermansia muciniphila at baseline, while Bifidobacterium longum was enriched at EOT (Figures S1 and S2). Dynamic treatment microbiome ecologic shifts, rather than fixed pretreatment profiles, may influence therapeutic response. This highlights the need for larger cohorts and more comprehensive functional and immune-based analyses. The future studies designed to evaluate whether microbiome features, functional pathways, or microbiome–immune interactions can serve as biomarkers of response or potential targets for microbiome-modulating interventions.

In a separately published article on 22 (69%) patients from this trial, 8 (36%) exhibited measurable 3D volumetric tumor reduction over sequential imaging intervals that correlated with disease control and completed chemotherapy cycles. Post-treatment imaging demonstrated shorter venous-phase perfusion times and reduced perfusion heterogeneity.27

Given the landmark 84% 6-month PFS and 58% ORR for the RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitor daraxonrasib with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel in untreated metastatic PDAC, NABPLAGEM plus paricalcitol plus RAS inhibition may increase efficacy in the neoadjuvant setting.28

Study limitations include a modest sample size at a single institution and not controlling for adjuvant therapies or surgical approaches. Nevertheless, these results support the feasibility, safety, and potential efficacy of combining NABPLAGEM with paricalcitol in neoadjuvant PDAC treatment and justify investigation particularly in understanding the impact of targeting VDR.
